criteria.label: Game design
criteria.description: Playability, fairness, feedback, pacing, visual readability, and how the mall and store mechanics work together.

criteria.label: Code architecture
criteria.description: Separation of rules and presentation, state ownership, determinism, module boundaries, and integration between systems.

criteria.label: Code design
criteria.description: Algorithms, data models, APIs, collision and input handling, correctness, and how easily the implementation can be extended.

criteria.label: Code cleanliness
criteria.description: Readability, naming, formatting, duplication, useful comments, type discipline, and removal of unfinished or disconnected code.

criteria.label: Prompt completeness
criteria.description: Working coverage of the original prompt: traversal, packages, stores, enemies, extras, power-ups, screens, audio, art, input, and technical constraints.

implementations.name: Claude Sonnet 5.5
implementations.note: A convincing mall: rich art, fair encounters, and broad coverage. Strong rule boundaries; the store module is oversized.

assessment.gameDesign: Detailed storefronts, lively characters, themed rooms, and clear search feedback make the caper feel coherent. Entry protection and guard delays improve fairness. Busy patterns and a dense HUD sometimes compete with the action.
assessment.architecture: A frame-driven Session owns the game flow; seeded rules and typed events are separated from browser, audio, and drawing. The boundaries are consistently exercised in Node. Some presentation state lives in the overlay rather than the simulation.
assessment.codeDesign: Input preserves printed-letter layouts and repeated taps; store movement, collision, searching, and guard behavior share explicit models. The roughly 1,200-line store module concentrates too many responsibilities despite otherwise focused modules.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict TypeScript, clear contracts, useful comments, and descriptive behavior tests make the implementation easy to follow. A few large modules and dense rendering code reduce local readability.
assessment.completeness: Very broad coverage of traversal, store extras, power-ups, generated art and music, and session screens. Its 477 tests include long seeded simulation runs. Sampled title, arrival, and store entry worked; this review did not establish a complete uninterrupted playthrough.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed

implementations.name: Claude Fable 5.1
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: Colorful, generous, and feature-rich, with dependable seeded rules. Large mall and store modules and busy floors limit polish.

assessment.gameDesign: Distinct stores, strong feedback, generous entry protection, and considerate search controls support the exploration loop. The busy floor patterns and compact HUD reduce readability in otherwise attractive scenes.
assessment.architecture: Pure frame-based game modules emit typed events to a separate renderer and audio layer. State and seeded setup are explicit. Type-only references to art and audio identities introduce mild coupling, and the mall module remains large.
assessment.codeDesign: Connected room layouts, accessible fixtures, corner assistance, and explicit interaction rules are thoughtfully implemented. The roughly 1,350-line mall and 650-line store modules would benefit from smaller responsibility boundaries.
assessment.cleanliness: Consistent strict TypeScript and readable names make the rules approachable. Comments explain deliberate gameplay choices. Long rule files and occasional tightly packed branches add maintenance cost.
assessment.completeness: The broad prompt coverage includes store-specific jokes, traversal, loot, powers, generated graphics, and sound. All 321 tests and the typechecked build passed. Browser sampling confirmed a real store transition and package search after preparing the player's position.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall, prepared store entry and package collection passed

implementations.name: Claude Opus 5
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, indexed framebuffer & WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A thorough, playable caper with strong palette rules and safety fixes. Huge rule files and injected callbacks complicate maintenance.

assessment.gameDesign: The mall and themed stores feel substantial, with useful feedback and safeguards against unavoidable spawn and ambush deaths. The detailed art is undermined slightly by busy backgrounds and a cramped HUD.
assessment.architecture: A pure core communicates through a typed EventBus; rendering and audio read state. Seeded frame timing and structural palette limits are strong choices. Globally injected transition callbacks and very large mall/store modules weaken isolation.
assessment.codeDesign: Collision, floor geometry, fixture reachability, elevator latches, and emergence grace receive careful treatment and regression coverage. The callback wiring and roughly 1,800-line mall module make extensions harder than the underlying models require.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict typing, centralized constants and copy, and comments explaining design decisions keep the implementation consistent. Long functions and files make it harder to trace a single interaction through the rules.
assessment.completeness: Extensive coverage of the game loop, store extras, powers, generated assets, and CRT requirements. All 217 tests and the typechecked build passed. Sampled title, mall, and prepared store entry worked; full-route completion was not independently replayed here.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed

implementations.name: Claude Opus 5.5
implementations.note: Rich arcade detail and focused rule modules. Pixi scenes own some scoring and timing, and busy rooms weaken visual clarity.

assessment.gameDesign: Recognizable characters, themed storefronts, and broad arcade interactions create an engaging world. Striped rooms and large speech text can obscure the action; the presentation is less legible than its feature coverage suggests.
assessment.architecture: Physics, elevators, combat, and store worlds have useful rule modules. However, Pixi scenes also own scoring, transition timing, and presentation state; mutable global store hooks introduce initialization dependencies. The pure boundary is incomplete.
assessment.codeDesign: Focused world updates, seeded content, and queued layout-aware input are good foundations. Scene-owned state and fixed store placement make independent simulation and larger-room extensions less straightforward.
assessment.cleanliness: Most modules are short, sensibly named, and supported by behavior tests. Task-number comments and scene/world overlap add noise, and untyped shared hooks provide weaker contracts than the strongest TypeScript entries.
assessment.completeness: A broad implementation with many mechanics, generated sprites and sounds, and a working sampled store transition. All 319 tests and the production build passed; a sizable portion of the suite validates assets. Scene coupling and room-camera limitations leave technical prompt gaps.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed

implementations.name: GPT-6.1 Sol
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D & WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A compact, broadly working game with useful route tests. One large rules file, simpler art, and uneven encounter protection hold it back.

assessment.gameDesign: Readable characters, clear package feedback, and functional movement support a convincing core loop. Store decoration is comparatively sparse, first-visit interruptions freeze the player, and ambush protection is less considerate than in the strongest entries.
assessment.architecture: The rules are pure and seeded, with separate drawing, input, and audio. A roughly 1,650-line game file owns most systems, and string events plus shared actor collections blur subsystem boundaries.
assessment.codeDesign: BFS navigation, fixture geometry, corner assistance, and explicit search controls are solid. A very broad Game state, short variable names, shared mall/store actors, and UI-string power identities make the model harder to extend.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict typing, a small dependency footprint, and useful verification documentation are strengths. Large files and compressed branches reduce readability, though the code is substantially clearer than the earlier Sol implementation.
assessment.completeness: Most gameplay systems, extras, powers, and generated audio are represented. All 75 tests and the typechecked build passed. Browser sampling confirmed prepared store entry and package collection. Art detail and some encounter behavior fall short of the most complete implementations.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall, prepared store entry and package collection passed

implementations.name: Claude Opus 4.6
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D with CRT effect, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A substantial core, but several features stop at emitted events. Simplified collisions, mismatched audio hooks, and dark art hurt play.

assessment.gameDesign: The sampled title, mall, and store transition work, and many arcade systems are present. Dark sprites, simplified room interactions, missing visible dialogue, and inconsistent hazard handling make the experience less convincing.
assessment.architecture: Seeded rules, event output, and separate rendering/audio form a sound outline. The roughly 2,500-line simulation and 1,850-line renderer duplicate geometry and behavior, while event names disagree with their consumers.
assessment.codeDesign: Store movement largely clamps to bounds instead of colliding with the rendered layout. Re-entry preserves dead guards, repeated taps collapse into booleans, and physical-key lookup takes precedence over printed letters. Several store extras emit events without implementing their intended interactions.
assessment.cleanliness: Conventional TypeScript formatting and descriptive names help navigation. Duplicated store initialization, large files, loose string events, and explanatory comments attached to incomplete behavior increase maintenance risk.
assessment.completeness: Many systems exist and all 219 tests plus the typechecked build passed. However, music and speech events are disconnected, store collision and extras are simplified, and level-clear scoring awards package points again. Passing tests overstate integration coverage.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed; presentation sampled

implementations.name: GPT-6 Sol
implementations.note: A recognizable, lightweight prototype. Compressed rules hide revived dead spies, loot gaps, weak collisions, and a very small sprite set.

assessment.gameDesign: The title, mall, and basic package loop are recognizable. Static sprites, simple rooms, and weak enemy behavior reduce the sense of a finished arcade game. Searching freezes store hazards, which distorts the intended risk and pacing.
assessment.architecture: Browser I/O, rendering, and seeded rules are separated, and updates clone state. Nearly all session, mall, and store rules are packed into one compressed module, with few explicit subsystem contracts.
assessment.codeDesign: A reproduced rule defect lets dead spies become active after their death timer expires. Black Friday shop generation leaves empty fixtures, guard movement ignores fixture collision, and the listening-booth geometry appears to prevent its activation. Cloning all state each tick adds unnecessary work.
assessment.cleanliness: Very long, densely compressed lines, single-letter locals, and combined responsibilities make inspection and safe changes difficult. The input module is more considered, but the overall source reads like a compressed prototype.
assessment.completeness: The basic screens and many named mechanics exist; all 25 tests and the build passed. Only six static gameplay sprites are defined, the CRT lacks real curvature, and several traversal, store, and power-up rules are partial or incorrect. The tests miss important gameplay defects.

verification.browser: Title, arrival and mall sampled; dead-spy and Black Friday defects reproduced in Node

implementations.name: Gemini 3.6 Flash
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D & WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: Readable scaffolding, but the game loop is unfinished: stores cannot be exited, elevators do not carry the agent, and combat is incomplete.

assessment.gameDesign: The mall renders and movement can be sampled, but essential progression is blocked. Store exits are unreachable, elevator movement does not carry the player, and minimal room art offers little feedback or atmosphere.
assessment.architecture: Logic, renderer, input, and synthesis are in separate modules. The boundary is weakened by non-seeded floating-text IDs, inconsistent private fixture data versus drawing, and incomplete integration of combat and traversal.
assessment.codeDesign: Store movement clamps the player's y position to 144 while exit requires more than 154; a browser probe reproduced the trap. Enemy bullets are created without a complete movement/collision path, and searches and fixtures lack the required collision and cancellation behavior.
assessment.cleanliness: Conventional formatting and recognizable module names make the scaffolding readable. Loose contracts, hardcoded room drawing, and unused or disconnected behavior obscure what actually works.
assessment.completeness: All 14 tests and the typechecked build passed, but essential traversal and combat, guards, many NPCs/extras, and distinct store experiences are missing or partial. The unreachable store exit prevents completing the requested package loop.

verification.browser: Title and mall sampled; prepared store exit stayed blocked at y=144

implementations.name: Claude Haiku 4.5
implementations.note: The browser never leaves frame zero. Readable pieces exist, but broken timing, disconnected elevators, and instant searches prevent play.

assessment.gameDesign: Normal launch stays on the first splash frame, including after Enter, so there is no usable player experience. Direct rule calls expose basic movement, but the store and traversal systems do not support the intended loop.
assessment.architecture: Modules suggest useful separation, but rules directly invoke audio, use unseeded randomness, and attach ad hoc store state. Elevator and power-up modules are not reliably integrated, and duplicate state fields disagree.
assessment.codeDesign: The main loop resets its timestamp whenever frame is zero, producing zero elapsed time forever. Elevator updates are not called by mall rules, store movement advances a tile per frame, and searches reveal contents immediately instead of running the specified timed interaction.
assessment.cleanliness: Formatting and straightforward names are readable. Placeholder comments, disconnected code, casts to any, and extensive TypeScript errors show that the pieces were not brought to a consistent finished state.
assessment.completeness: The 13 unit tests and Vite build passed, but a separate TypeScript check failed. The browser is stuck at frame zero; guards, collision, progression, and multiple extras are absent or incomplete. The existing tests exercise isolated rules and miss the broken entry point.

verification.build: Vite build passes; separate TypeScript check fails
verification.browser: Splash remained at frame zero before and after Enter

implementations.name: Claude Haiku 5.5
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D with a row-based CRT effect, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A complete, playable caper with clean rule boundaries. Power-ups never expire, the map breaks stores, and Game Over hides behind shutters.

assessment.gameDesign: The whole loop plays: zip-line arrival, elevators and escalators, timed searches with a progress bar, banners and popups, first-visit lines, level clear and harder loops, with telegraphed shots, store grace and respawn invulnerability for fairness. Opening the map inside a store leaves the room frozen on screen while the mall rules keep moving the agent, the wet-floor slide applies on every floor and can block the getaway wagon, timed power-ups never run out, and the Game Over screen ends fully covered by its shutters. Dark backdrops, abstract window displays and overflowing two-line signs make the mall less readable than the strongest entries.
assessment.architecture: Pure, seeded rules in core, mall and store modules emit typed events that a state-reading renderer and an audio layer consume; the input mapper and the splash are standalone and the browser shell is thin. The roughly 1,450-line mall module concentrates most behaviour, the game never ticks the power-up timers it owns, the map screen ignores which screen opened it, and banners persist across scene changes. Debug mode pauses real time, so the hooks cannot observe live play.
assessment.codeDesign: The elevator state machine, printed-letter input with exact key release and a tap queue, tile collision with corner assist, and once-per-volley dodge rolls are well modelled. The wet-floor check ignores floors, closing the map inside a store returns to the mall with the room still attached, timed power-ups last until death, the shutter animation covers the Game Over text, and the room system is fixed at 16 by 11 tiles without a camera.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict TypeScript with no escape hatches, short focused modules outside the mall world, readable names, and comments that explain gameplay decisions. Copy is duplicated inside rule modules despite the stated single-source rule, several sound effects, the shake output and some copy constants are defined but never used, and the README contradicts itself about the browser playtest.
assessment.completeness: Nearly every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, with 115 tests across the listed rule areas; the strict build and the published sub-path deployment work, and browser checks logged no console errors. Real-time play covered splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, the map, pause and the CRT and mute toggles; stepped checks covered store entry, a package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over. The unticked power-up timers, the map inside stores, the floor-blind wet patch and the hidden Game Over text are working-coverage gaps; the room camera, photo strip and automatic-car ride are simplified.

verification.browser: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, map, pause and toggles passed; prepared store entry, package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over stepped; map-in-store, wet-floor and shutter defects reproduced

evidence.label: Map screen returns to the mall

implementations.name: Claude Sonnet 5.5 + Fable 5.1 advisor
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, software framebuffer with a WebGL CRT presenter, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: The most legible mall and the first full route replayed in the live build. Plug-in mall modules; two 1,200-line worlds remain.

assessment.gameDesign: Clean, readable storefronts with a wide corridor palette, a legible HUD with an LED floor panel and scrolling store marquee, and well-staged screens: a SPYGRAM card, a receipt-style tally, THE DAILY MALL, a vector-grid continue countdown and typewriter shutters at game over. Elevators glide, floor banners announce, the directory map is clear and shows the current store from inside a room. Fairness was tuned with scripted players over 40 seeds, not with a human. A cleared or closed store door gives no feedback on Up, and the Black Friday flash overlaps the copyright line on the title. Survivability by a human was not tested here.
assessment.architecture: A scene machine (Game) owns a Level that holds the mall, the current store, the overlays and the fades, so the map and pause work identically in both views. Rules are pure and frame-based, emit sound requests through the Run and expose music through state; a grep test keeps the rule layers free of the DOM, Math.random and timers. Mall extras (lamps, janitor, walkers, cop, kiosks, booth, fountains) are plug-in modules with typed state the renderer reads, which keeps the core world smaller than its siblings. The mall and store worlds are still about 1,200 lines each.
assessment.codeDesign: The elevator model (drive, glide, call protection, occupancy, grate and pit states), shaft-wall door windows, tile collision with corner assist, a tap queue that preserves fast taps across catch-up steps, and a store room system that already supports any size with a camera are all well modelled and tested. A scripted player that only presses buttons doubles as a routing proof and a fairness probe. Spy AI is deliberately simple, the cop ignores escalators, and a few interactions fall through silently.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict TypeScript with no escape hatches, no stray TODOs or console calls, every line of copy in one module with fit tests, named constants for all timings, and comments that explain gameplay decisions. The README and AGENTS.md are precise about what was and was not verified. There is no lint or format configuration and unused locals are not flagged, and the two world modules are long.
assessment.completeness: Every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, and 754 tests cover rules, art contracts, music theory and seeded playthroughs. This review drove the branch's own scripted player, kept invulnerable, through the whole route in the published sub-path build, which proves routing and screen flow rather than survivability: splash, title, arrival, walking, an elevator ride and escalator, a lamp shot, all six package stores, the refused re-entry of a cleared store, the exit firing once, the tally, newspaper and post, a harder loop 2, continue, game over, the Konami code and the GameStonk easter egg, with an empty console. Music was checked numerically by the author and not listened to here.

verification.browser: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator ride, floor banner, CRT and mute toggles, map and pause passed on the published build; stepped checks with the scripted player kept invulnerable completed the full six-package route to level clear, loop 2, continue, game over, Konami, easter egg, map inside a store, escalator and lamp shot with no console messages

implementations.name: Claude Sonnet 5.5 + Opus 5.5 advisor
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D with a WebGL CRT presenter, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A legible mall whose own bot finished the live route without dying. Untyped events, unused-import hacks, and car deaths respawn far away.

assessment.gameDesign: Clean pastel storefronts whose windows read at a glance, a wide corridor palette, a 16 px HUD with an LED floor panel and a store marquee, a floor banner on every stop, and well-staged screens: the SPYGRAM card, a MISSION COMPLETE drive-off with the receipt-waving spy, a receipt-style tally, THE DAILY MALL and a typewriter message that stays readable over the game-over shutters. Searching is forgiving, with a progress bar under the store name. Fairness was tuned with a non-dodging bot over 24 seeds, and the same bot finished loop 1 on seed 5 in the live build without a death. The safe spot is never updated while riding, so a death inside an elevator car respawns the agent where it boarded; in real-time play a death at 2F sent the agent back to the roof. Checkerboard store floors are busier than the mall.
assessment.architecture: A Game state machine owns a RunState shared by the mall and the stores, a Mall and a StoreRoom; the map and pause remember which view is underneath, power-up timers tick in both views and stop on the overlays. The rules layer has no DOM, timers or Math.random, by inspection rather than a guard test, and emits plain events through one queue; the renderer keeps its own door, popup and toast state clocked by simulation frames, so visuals do not depend on the display refresh rate. Spies and NPCs are split out of the 1,300-line mall module and the store room system takes any size with a camera. Event payloads are untyped and consumers cast them.
assessment.codeDesign: The elevator model (glide, one ding per stop, call protection, grate, pit and roof states), the input mapper with printed-letter bindings, exact release and a tap queue, tile collision with corner assist, once-per-volley spy dodges, lamps placed by computing the corridor gaps from the geometry, and a goal-based BFS bot that doubles as a softlock detector are all well modelled and tested. The safe-spot rule ignores elevator rides, spy AI is simple, the cop ignores escalators, and one hazard check carries an empty branch.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict TypeScript, every line of copy in one module with fit tests, named frame constants, comments that explain decisions, and a README and AGENTS.md that record the advisor consultations and the gotchas. Unused locals are not flagged, so a dozen void statements silence unused imports; event data is typed as any, there is a placeholder draw call and an empty if block, and there is no lint or format configuration.
assessment.completeness: Every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, and 240 tests cover rules, input layouts, art contracts, songs, copy fit, refresh-rate timing, a 24-seed fairness run and a scripted full level on 8 seeds. This review played the published sub-path build in real time through splash, title, arrival, walking, an elevator ride, the map, pause and the CRT and mute toggles, then drove the branch's own scripted bot, left vulnerable, through the full six-package route on seed 5 to level clear, THE DAILY MALL, the post and loop 2 with no deaths, matching the Node trajectory frame for frame; continue, game over, the Konami code, the GameStonk cave, the map inside a store, an escalator ride and a lamp shot were stepped, with an empty console. Music was not listened to.

verification.browser: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator ride, floor banner, map, pause, CRT and mute toggles passed on the published build; the branch's scripted bot, left vulnerable, completed the full six-package route to level clear and loop 2 with no deaths; continue, game over, Konami, GameStonk cave, map inside a store, escalator and lamp shot stepped with no console messages; the roof respawn after a death inside a car was seen live and reproduced in Node

implementations.name: GPT-6 Astra
implementations.technology: Vanilla JavaScript modules with no dependencies, Canvas 2D with a WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A complete, legible mall with no dependencies, built in forty minutes. Store rooms are flat identical grids; songs are eight-note loops.

assessment.gameDesign: The mall reads well at NES scale: every storefront shows its goods in the windows, blinking red doors mark the targets, closed shops carry FOR LEASE and CLOSING SALE shutters, floors are labelled, and the elevator cars have doors that close while moving. The title screen, the SPYGRAM cards, the kiosk panel, the photo strip, MISSION COMPLETE with the receipt-waving spy, THE DAILY MALL and the shutters rolling down over the mall at game over are all staged with care. The stores let it down: all ten rooms are the same 16 by 11 checkerboard with eight identical fixture boxes topped by one sprite per theme, no counters or walls, and two guards at fixed positions, so the Zelda half of the game is a flat grid. Music is one monophonic eight-note loop per track over a bass and a triangle, so the ten store songs are barely distinguishable. The banner box covers the store name header, the agent holds a package overhead after an empty or trapped search, and the Black Friday sign on the title is clipped by the storefront row.
assessment.architecture: A 1,782-line rules module owns the whole simulation as a plain state object stepped at 60 Hz with the state's own xorshift PRNG and no DOM, timers or Math.random; it emits events that the audio layer consumes, and the renderer only reads state. The fixed loop caps catch-up at five steps, the input layer merges keyboard and gamepad into held and pressed sets with a tap queue that survives catch-up, and the browser adapter is 175 lines. The room system clamps a camera to the room size, so bigger rooms would work, but nothing else is modular: mall, store, elevators, NPCs, lamps, scoring and screens all share one file, and the renderer imports the rules module to ask which fixture is touched.
assessment.codeDesign: The elevator model (floor-to-floor glide, one ding per stop, called cars that pick up instead of crush, the automatic car waiting for an occupant), the printed-letter input mapping with release by physical key, the forgiving touch-based search and the once-per-volley spy dodge are modelled cleanly and each has a test. Against that, the code is terse to a fault: state, player, elevator and fixture are s, p, e and f throughout, positions such as the wagon at 626, the booth at 410 and the kiosks at 384 are bare literals, and fixture contents are chosen by a ternary nested five deep. The search pose is reused for every outcome, which is why the agent lifts a package he did not find.
assessment.cleanliness: Prettier-style formatting is consistent, every line of copy sits in one module with a fit test, and the README and AGENTS.md are short and honest, including the note that the run began inside an existing conversation rather than a fresh session. There is no type checking, no lint configuration and almost no commenting, and the single-letter naming makes the rules file hard to scan. Tests are 56 broad cases in two files, several asserting a dozen things each.
assessment.completeness: Every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option in the brief is present, and 56 tests cover the fixed step, input layouts, the art pipeline, room reachability, elevators, scoring, power-up timers, NPCs, the Konami code, spy fairness, searching, the extras, the exit rule, continues, splash timing and copy limits. This review stepped the published sub-path build through its debug hook with the CRT on: splash, title, arrival and selfie, an elevator ride with its floor banner, a store visit with the first-visit lines, a search, the map and pause, a spy kill with last words, a falling lamp, an escalator, the kiosk, the photo booth, the fountain, the wet floor, the mall cop's detention, death and respawn, continue, game over, the Konami code and Black Friday signs, the GameStonk cave, the parking level, level clear, the newspaper, the post, loop 2, the CRT and mute toggles and the sprite gallery, with an empty console. Real-time keyboard play and the music were not checked by this review; the branch README reports its own real-time run. Store themes differ only by palette, Circuit Pity shows FOR LEASE instead of a half-open shutter, and guards are always two.

verification.build: Pass; no dependencies, static copy to dist/

implementations.name: Kimi K3.1 Pro (high)
implementations.technology: Vanilla JavaScript + Vite, Canvas 2D with a CSS CRT overlay, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: Every screen is there on a tidy rules core, but car roofs drop the agent out of the world and the roof start kills most first walks.

assessment.gameDesign: The screen flow is staged with care: the FLICKERSOFT flicker, a night-sky title, the zip line onto the roof, a SPYGRAM selfie card with climbing likes, floor banners on every elevator stop, a parking-garage tally with the receipt-waving spy, THE DAILY MALL, the mission post and shutters rolling down at game over. Play breaks down in the elevator shafts. A drop into a pit with the car one floor below lands the agent on its roof, but the roof is not tracked as a platform: when the car rises, and the brief's half-second auto-call raises it as soon as the agent stands still there, the agent falls through it and keeps falling forever with no death. That happens on a natural route (ride B from 4F to 3F, take the escalator back up, walk to B and wait), and the only escape is pressing Up blind at an open store door on that floor. Shaft B is drawn behind the Forever 12, KGB Toys and Sam Baddy facades, so its pit is invisible on 4F to 2F. Walking right from the start toward elevator A drops the agent into automatic car C's pit on the roof in 28 of 40 seeds, and jumping cannot clear an opening, so most first walks end in a death. Hiding in the photo booth does not protect from spy contact, standing in car C's open doorway is a crush when it leaves downward, and spies spawn at store doors anywhere on an adjacent floor, so four can be waiting on 4F before the agent leaves the roof. Store rooms are one 16 by 11 grid of identical boxes with a few rows moved per store; both windows of a storefront show the same display; two-line signs collide with the Black Friday banner, the 3F kiosk is drawn over Blockbluster's shutter and the newspaper's column rules run past the page.
assessment.architecture: The rules live in src/core as plain modules with no DOM, Canvas, timers or Math.random: one seeded xorshift stream, frame counters for every duration, a fixed-step accumulator capped at five catch-up steps, and events as the only route to sound and screen effects. Elevators, physics, searching, power-ups, scoring, input and copy are separate small modules, and the store renderer clamps a camera to the template size. The 899-line MallGame class still owns the mall, the stores, NPCs, lamps, screens and the scene machine in one place; main.js writes the CRT and sound notices into the rules state, and the renderer imports a rules helper it never uses.
assessment.codeDesign: The input pad releases the exact physical token, queues taps across catch-up steps and maps letters by printed key; elevator stops ding once on the moving-to-stopped edge, called cars do not crush their caller, and the Konami detector forgives leading Ups. The shaft logic is where it fails: the pit check re-arms every frame, the landing height follows the car only while the agent is over the opening, and integrateVertical lands only when the feet cross the target from above, so once a rising car passes the agent's feet no landing line is ever crossed again; stepping off a roof sideways snaps the agent back up to the floor it fell from. fallStartY means the head on a jump and the feet on a pit drop. Spy contact ignores the hidden flag, the automatic car counts only a boarded rider as an occupant, the cop teleports to the agent's floor every two seconds, and corner assist is a one-pixel nudge while the exported cornerAssist helper goes unused.
assessment.cleanliness: Modules are short and named for what they do, every line of copy sits in copy.js with fit tests, and the README, AGENTS.md and DECISIONS.md are honest about how the run went and what the playtest shortcuts. The two largest files pack several statements per line, with 41 lines over 180 characters in game.js and renderer.js; there are no types, no lint and few comments, a ternary that returns square either way, and unused exports (EVENT, approach, floorAtY, STORE_W, HUD_H, cornerAssist). The pages workflow still lists main as a trigger branch. Tests are 64 compact cases in six files.
assessment.completeness: Every screen, the Konami code with Black Friday, the map with car positions and radar marks, pause, continues, game over, the gallery, the debug hooks, the kiosks, photo booth, fountains, lamps and disco balls, janitor, walkers, cop, the fitting room, toy shelf, listening booth and GameStonk cave are present, and 64 tests cover most of section 11. Missing or thin: the 1-Up never appears (no shop or spy drop holds one, 0 of 33,034 fixtures over 199 seeds), riding a car roof does not work, spies never wait at shaft openings, there is no elevator hum, the kiosk answers with a text line instead of a map panel and the photo strip is a message. All ten store songs are one eight-note arpeggio transposed per store, several effects use a sawtooth outside the NES channel set, and the music was not listened to. This review drove the published sub-path build in headless Chrome over the DevTools protocol, in real time with key events and the CRT on: splash, title, Konami code, zip line, selfie, a death in car C's roof pit, calling C, boarding A and riding it to the 4F banner, a lost life on 4F of unrecorded cause, Radioshock entry, single-tap searches through a trap, a Spread Shot, a NOTHING HERE and the package, the map, pause, CRT and mute toggles, the GameStonk cave and its joke item, the blocked exit, then level clear from six packages set by hand, the newspaper, the post, loop 2, continue, game over and the gallery, with an empty console. No spy kill or lamp shot was confirmed live.

implementations.note: Readable, separated rules, but elevators trap the agent and stores eject them immediately. All 60 tests pass; the build fails.

assessment.gameDesign: The splash, title, zip-line arrival and selfie establish the premise, but ordinary progression is blocked. In real-time keyboard play, boarding elevator A left the agent at the roof: holding Down never moved the car, and Right could not leave it. After preparing a position at Forever 12, pressing Up entered the store for one simulation frame and immediately returned to the mall, even with Up held. The player spawns on the exit tile and cannot move far enough off it before the exit check. A package could be searched only after moving the player beside its fixture through the debug state and removing guards. Storefront windows are plain rectangles, signs are truncated to ten characters, and all store palettes fall back to the same gadget theme because the renderer looks up a store ID in a theme-keyed table. Screenshots show a clipped floor HUD and a black pause screen instead of a dimmed scene. These are fundamental playability and presentation gaps, rather than a difficult but complete game.
assessment.architecture: The strongest part is a real separation between pure seeded rules, Canvas drawing, browser input and Web Audio. Game owns session state and dispatches to separate mall and store modules; the renderer reads state and events drive sound. The fixed 60 Hz accumulator caps catch-up at five steps. However, event names and payloads are loosely typed, nearly all mall behavior shares one large module, and power-up ownership is split awkwardly: effects live on the mall player while the store has a different player and never advances those timers. Store state is recreated on every entry, so there is no durable per-level room state or per-game visit history. The module boundaries are useful, but missing integration prevents several declared systems from functioning.
assessment.codeDesign: Manual elevator input never sets a destination or movement direction, no code handles leaving a boarded car, and automatic-car updates do not carry the rider. The store spawn/exit geometry is incompatible. Probes also confirmed that a 1,200-frame weapon timer remains at 1,200 after 120 store steps, opened fixtures reset on re-entry, the GameStonk reward is granted again on every entry, and an aligned store spy stays at aim timer 30 for 240 frames without firing. Loop 2 retains all six collected packages and therefore keeps target stores cleared; level clear adds another 3,000 package points after collection already awards them. Continuing recreates the mall at the roof instead of resuming where the agent fell. Black Friday still generates traps and empty fixtures. Printed-letter keyboard mapping and physical-key release tracking work in isolation, but an idle connected gamepad clears keyboard-held buttons, and disconnecting a held gamepad leaves them stuck. Jumping has no horizontal movement while airborne, Spread Shot's normal two-bullet cap truncates its three shots, player bullets never trigger falling lamps, and spy-contact/jump-kick collisions are absent.
assessment.cleanliness: Names, formatting, section comments and explicit TypeScript state interfaces make the source substantially easier to inspect than compressed prototype entries. The dependency footprint is small and DECISIONS.md candidly lists some omissions. There is nevertheless considerable unfinished scaffolding: identical walk/jump sprite frames, unused store-extra fields, an identical-result bot sprite ternary, and comments claiming behavior that is not wired. Copy is not fully centralized. The suite has 60 passing cases, but its reachability test checks a graph of declared floors rather than operating elevators, and search tests move the player directly to fixtures, bypassing the broken entrance. The README's successful-build and complete-core-loop claims are contradicted by this snapshot: strict compilation fails in test/copy.test.ts:16 (possibly undefined line) and test/sprites.test.ts:52 (implicit-any callback parameter), matching the failed CI run.
assessment.completeness: There are thirteen storefront definitions, room layouts, seeded loot, scoring and power-up APIs, a map, pause, Konami detection, continue/game-over screens and the level-clear/headline/post sequence. Those pieces do not produce the required start-to-finish game: elevator travel and ordinary store entry are blocked, and the production build cannot deploy. Missing or partial systems include elevator calls, roof riding and crushing, store spy shooting, fitting rooms, wind-up toys, listening booths, the full GameStonk cave, fountain coin creation, photo strips, wet-floor sliding, walker penalties, working lamp shots/disco balls, radar marks, animated shop displays and the getaway-car scene. Store music is one shared eight-note pattern; the splash is embedded in Game/Renderer rather than a reusable module; CRT curvature is absent. Real-time browser checks used the local development server, not a published or production build. Prepared state reached one package and the closing screens; no full route is claimed. No game JavaScript exception was observed, but favicon requests returned 404s. The gallery and CRT/mute controls were sampled; music was inspected in source, not listened to.
